messages.subject: Re: full.scores.SE=TRUE in fscore()
messages.body_plain:
Hi Michael,

ML estimates of θ are generally much wider than the Bayes cousins since they depend only on the vector of observations and model to inform the estimates. For multidimensional models this can be a big issue as well since if very few items load on a given factor then there will be very little information about the θ estimate (often less than the total number of items). I suspect that is what is happening in your case; you may just have weakly informed factors, which in turn lead to weakly informed factor score estimates. HTH.

Phil

messages.subject: Is the Item Category Information Function correctly defined?
messages.subject_clean: Is the Item Category Information Function correctly defined?
messages.body_plain:
Phil,

in your ItemInfo/ItemInfo2 functions, the category information is calculated as grad^2/P per category, and the item information (if total.info <http://total.info> is set to TRUE) as the sum across categories:

 for(i in seq_len(x@ncat))
        info[,i] <- (dx$grad[[i]])^2 / P[ ,i]
     if(total.info <http://total.info>) info <- rowSums(info)

 for(i in seq_len(x@ncat))
            info <- info + outer(as.numeric(dx$grad[[i]]), as.numeric(dx$grad[[i]])) / P[ ,i]

Following Samejima (1969), the category information function (or item response information function) is minus the second derivative of the log of the category probability, yielding

I = (P')^2/P - P''

with I for information and P' denoting the first and P'' the second derivative of P (each carrying an index for the item and the category; see also Magis, 2015, Eq. 8).

Now, Samejima (1969, p.39, Eq. 6-7) shows that for the item information, the P'' part of the equation above can be omitted, as it sums up to zero across categories (see also O&N2006, p.69, Eq. 4.13 and above). However, this is not the case for the categories' information. Hence, shouldn't the item category information curves include the P'' part as well?

The difference is that the category information functions are (usually) unimodal if P'' is included (cf. Samejima, 1969, p.40, Fig. 6-2) but bimodal if not, thus exhibiting entirely different shapes.

Thank you,
Milica

Refs:
Magis (2015) DOI: 10.3102/1076998614558122
Ostini & Nering (2006) DOI: 10.4135/9781412985413
Samejima (1969) DOI: 10.1007/BF03372160

messages.subject: could mirt accept sparse data matrix and/or data in long format?
messages.subject_clean: could mirt accept sparse data matrix and/or data in long format?
messages.body_plain:
I am dealing with a rather large data set (some millions of users, some tens of thousands of items). The data is sparse, so when user-actions are recorded in a long format, it is of manageable size. But to send this data to mirt() requires converting it to a dense matrix. For my data size it means running out of memory, so I am forced to sub-sample the data. I can't help wondering whether mirt() could skip the dense-matrix step and accept either data-frames in long format or (which is essentially the same) sparse matrices. Are there any plans to develop this?

Thank you,
Ilia

messages.subject: Re: full.scores.SE=TRUE in fscore()
messages.body_plain:
Hi Michael,

That doesn't sound unreasonable to me (precise measurement of latent variables is hard). The SEs themselves are just a function of the inverse of the observed information function at the MLE. Note that if you have lower discrimination/slope parameters this can happen to an even worse degree. Consider the following example, which gives mean(SE) ~= .47.  This is partially why computerized adaptive testing is so useful in reducing the length of a test as a function of the size and information available in an item bank. HTH.

Phil

###
library(mirt)
a <- rlnorm(150, -1, .3)
d <- rnorm(150, sd=2)

mean(a)

dat <- simdata(a, d, N=5000, itemtype = '2PL')
(mod <- mirt(dat))
fs <- fscores(mod, full.scores.SE <http://full.scores.SE> = TRUE)
round(colMeans(fs), 3)
####

messages.subject: Re: Dynamic thurstonian model using mirt - is it possible?
messages.subject_clean: Dynamic thurstonian model using mirt - is it possible?
messages.body_plain:
Dear Phil,

I apologize for the delay; my spam filter decided I shouldn't receive your response, and I wasn't checking here online. We are doing a re-analysis of the OMT test, the original paper here:

Runge, J. M., Lang, J. W., Engeser, S., Schüler, J., den Hartog, S. C., & Zettler, I. (2016). Modeling motive activation in the Operant Motive Test: A psychometric analysis using dynamic Thurstonian item response theory. Motivation Science, 2(4), 268. https://doi.org/10.1037/mot0000041 <https://psycnet.apa.org/doi/10.1037/mot0000041>

The lme4 model is described there (models M3 and M4), but their description is too complicated.

However, I solved the problem in the meantime using two different approaches.
Using a bifactor structure with specific factors, which model residual dependency between items.
Defining my item response function using createSyntax function, which is fantastic! I provided additional covdata, which does the job.

Unfortunately, we probably won't use these more advanced models in our paper, and I stopped elaborating on them a few months ago. The data are messy anyway; and while even the simplest model fits them very well, the reliability is negligible.

messages.subject: Re: Item information matrix
messages.body_plain:
Dear Phil,
Thank you for the detailed response again; I hate my spam folder!
I solved the problem successfully; we soon realized that in a multidimensional setting, an information matrix cannot be used to estimate measurement errors. Unfortunately, estimating the Hessian matrix in Python with acceptable numerical stability was terrible. Thank you for having mirt as a benchmark!

Dne pondělí 16. ledna 2023 v 21:31:14 UTC+1 uživatel rphilip....@gmail.com napsal:

> Hi Hynek,
>
>
> On Tue, Mar 22, 2022 at 9:04 AM Hynek Cígler <cigler...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Hello,
> > I have several questions concerning the item information matrix and selection criteria used in mirt and mirtCAT. These could be elementary questions for somebody here, but I am - as a non-statistician - struggling :-) All the questions are related to a confirmatory multidimensional model with correlated traits, where each item has only one or two non-zero loadings.
> >
> > First of all, I have a problem conceptually understanding what do the off-diagonal elements of the item information matrix (IIM) represent. Is it un uncertainty related to the difference (or trade-off) between two thetas estimates?
>
> The off-diagonal elements have to do with whether the item correlates with both traits (i.e., has non-zero slopes for each), in which case the item will measures something about more than one variable (diagonal terms) with some degree of shared information (off-diagonal). Items containing only one unique loading will have zers everywhere except their respective diagonal.
>
>
> >
> >
> > Second, I want to estimate information in the direction of the single dimension. Therefore, the angle between this single direction and my dimension is zero. Thus the weight of a particular element in IIM will be 1 (as the cos(0) = 1 = r). But what about the other dimensions? Will these weights be zero, or should I add the factor correlation?
>
> You would want set the weights of the other dimensions to zero, though rarely is this something that I recommend doing (unless you are searching for some maximal multidimensional information location, in which case MDIFF is the answer).
>
>
> > An example: I have two traits correlated r = 0.5. An item has the two factor loadings a_1 = 0.6 and a_2 = 0.7. The item information matrix would be
> >
> >
> > If I consider the angle 0 and 90 (r = {r_1 = 1, r_2 = 0}), the weighted IIM would be
> >
> > However, the traits are correlated, r = .5. Therefore, the question is whether angles 0 and 90 degrees are admissible. Shouldn't I use angles r = {r_1 = 1, r_2 = .5}, where the second angle represents the correlation of both traits? In such a case, IIM would be equal to
> >
> >
> > The latter gives me a sense as off-diagonals are related to discriminations between traits, and therefore, they are not zero. With highly correlated traits, off-diagonals elements will be close to zero, representing the inability to discriminate between correlated dimensions, and vice versa. However, an item could add information even in the factor with zero loading in the latter. Is it correct?
>
> This sounds correct from what I gather you're trying to do. Unidimensional items still provide information about other latent traits if indeed the traits are modeled to be correlated.
>
> >
> > The other question is related to item selection criteria. I did not find any documentation of them, so I ask here:
>
> Did you refer to the associated JSS article?
>
> > D-rule (IIM determinant) - this maximalize the ability to estimate each trait and discriminate between them, as it uses the whole information matrix?
> Yes, and analogously minimizes the expected measurement error by way of the determinant geometry.
> > T-rule (IIm diagonal) - this maximalize only the ability to estimate each trait, as it does not consider the off-diagonal elements?
>
> Correct.
>
> > A-rule (covariance matrix diagonal) - similar to T-rule, but work with an error matrix (inversed item information matrix)?
> Yes, and can behave differently (arguably, more optimally) when user-defined weights are included.
> > E-rule: I do not understand here. In mirt help, it is written: "the minimum value of the information matrix". Why does anybody want to use that?
> You generally don't, unless you're looking to uniformly minimize the general variance of the trait estimates.
>
> > W-rule: the same here. What means "the weighted information criteria"? Shouldn't be here a "weighted information matrix"?
>
> Is there a difference? Weights are applied to the information matrix to result in a scalar.
>
> >
> > Finally, for D-rule, T-rule, and E-rule, it is written "potentially weighted matrix". The matrix is therefore weighted using factors correlation matrix, right?
>
> Not quite, these are based on user-defined weights, where you may be working with a multidimensional test but really only want to select items that pertain to a specific dimension (such as the general factor in a bi-factor model). HTH.
>
> Phil

messages.subject: Bug in empirical reliability estimates using ML/WLE scores
messages.subject_clean: Bug in empirical reliability estimates using ML/WLE scores
messages.body_plain:
Hello,
I am afraid I found an error in reliability estimates using fscores(... , returnER = T, method = "ML"). If it's not an error, I don't understand the differences between methods, and I would be glad if anybody could explain it (I have some reasons for using WLE in norm construction and I don't want to report wrong reliability estimates).

The implemented equation for reliability is

A. r_xx = var(theta) / (var(theta) + RMSE**2)

This is correct if the estimation methods are EAP or MAP. However, I suppose for ML or WLE estimators, different equation should be used:

B. r_xx = (var(theta) - RMSE) / var(theta) = 1 - RMSE**2/var(theta)

With EAP or MAP, the estimates are regressed towards the mean; in terms of CTT, they are estimates of the true score (the most plausible score given the data assuming the person was randomly chosen from the population). Therefore, var(theta) is the variance of "true scores", and equation A is correct.

On the other hand, with ML or WLE, the estimates are not regressed toward the mean, and the score is the most plausible value given the data only. Therefore, var(theta) is the variance of "observed scores", and so equation B is correct instead.

I remember that in past mirt versions, equation B was used with ML/WLE estimator. Do I remember well? If so, why was it changed?

Reliabilities of different estimators shouldn't differ substantively. So, I tried the following script. While equation A for EAP/MAP and equation B for ML/WLE provides similar results (similar also to alpha for sum scores), equation A for ML/WLE seems to overestimate reliability.

library(mirt)
dat <- Science[rowSums(Science) != 4 & rowSums(Science) != 16, ]  ## exclude extreme cases

fit <- mirt(dat, model = 1, SE = T, itemtype = "Rasch")
fscores(fit, method = "EAP", returnER = T) ## 0.4926801
fscores(fit, method = "MAP", returnER = T) ## 0.4926442
fscores(fit, method = "ML", returnER = T)  ## 0.666287 - massive difference
fscores(fit, method = "WLE", returnER = T) ## 0.6590622 - massive difference

## Compute in hand - first, estimate scores
x <- fscores(fit, method = "ML", returnER = F, full.scores.SE <http://full.scores.SE> = T)
y <- fscores(fit, method = "WLE", returnER = F, full.scores.SE <http://full.scores.SE> = T)

var(x[,1])/(var(x[,1]) + mean(x[,2]**2)) ## 0.666287 - actual approach
var(y[,1])/(var(y[,1]) + mean(y[,2]**2)) ## 0.6590622 - actual approach

1 - mean(x[,2]**2)/var(x[,1]) ## 0.4991453 - correct approach? Similar to EAP/MAP
1 - mean(y[,2]**2)/var(y[,1]) ## 0.4826924 - correct approach? Similar to EAP/MAP

psych::alpha(dat)$total ## Finally, alpha for sum score is - again -  0.485212

Phil

messages.subject: IRT Poisson model
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I have been trying to implemente the following model (a particular model of that presented in https://cdr.lib.unc.edu/downloads/xd07gt356, Equation 3, when pij=1):

Y_{ij} ~ Poisson(lambda_{ij})
lambda_{ij} = exp(a_i(theta_j-b_i))

where theta_j, a_i, b_i play, essentially, the same role as in the 2PL usual model (for binary response). Then, I have written the following code:

_______________________________________________________________________________________
name <- 'C2PLPoi'
par <- c(a = .5, b = -2)
est <- c(TRUE, TRUE)
P.C2PLPoi <- function(par,Theta,ncat=Inf,itemdata){
  a <- par[1]
  b <- par[2]
  y<-itemdata
  lambda <- exp(a*(Theta-b))
  P <- dpois(y,lambda)
  P
}

mC2PLPoi<-createItem(name, par=par, est=est,
                     P=P.C2PLPoi)

a<- abs(rnorm(10))
b <- rnorm(10)
theta <- rnorm(500)
mlambda<-matrix(exp(a*(theta-b)),500,10)
mY <- matrix(0,500,10)
for(r in 1:10){
mY[,r] <- rpois(n=500,lambda=mlambda[,r])
}

_______________________________________________________________________________________

Then, I have execetude the above code, in two different ways, with the respective message errors also presented:

1)
mirt(mY, 1, 'mC2PLPoi', customItems=list(mC2PLPoi=mC2PLPoi))

"I1" re-mapped to ensure all categories have a distance of 1 "I2" re-mapped to ensure all categories have a distance of 1 "I3" re-mapped to ensure all categories have a distance of 1 "I4" re-mapped to ensure all categories have a distance of 1 "I5" re-mapped to ensure all categories have a distance of 1 "I6" re-mapped to ensure all categories have a distance of 1 "I7" re-mapped to ensure all categories have a distance of 1 "I8" re-mapped to ensure all categories have a distance of 1 "I9" re-mapped to ensure all categories have a distance of 1 "I10" re-mapped to ensure all categories have a distance of 1 Error in dpois(y, lambda) : Non numeric argument for a mathematical function In addition: Warning message: The following items have a large number of categories which may cause estimation issues: 2 4 8 9 10

_______________________________________________________________________________________

2)
mY <- remap.distance(mY)
mirt(mY, 1, 'mC2PLPoi', customItems=list(mC2PLPoi=mC2PLPoi))

Error in dpois(y, lambda) : Non numeric argument for a mathematical function In addition: Warning message: The following items have a large number of categories which may cause estimation issues: 2 4 8 9 10
_______________________________________________________________________________________

I Think that, essentially, those issues are due that the model has an "infinite number of categories" and, the, it is not possible to implement through mirt.

Any help is welcome,

Best,

Caio

messages.subject: Re: IRT Poisson model
messages.body_plain:
Hi Caio,

I'm afraid count data is not easily supported by this function, as the table of expected counts is positively unbounded; hence, the expectation tables would need to account for each unique count in the complete dataset, which makes the E-table quite massive. There is, however, the countirt package to perform such analyses (https://github.com/mbsmn/countirt), which you may find helpful. It's possible that I'll add count IRT models to mirt in the future, but this is low on my TODO list. Cheers.

Phil
